title: Parametric and symmetric equations of lines
section: Analytic Geometry of R3 ▷ Lines in 3-Space
terms: line in space; direction vector; parametric equations; symmetric equations; skew lines.

exposition.text:
A line through P with nonzero direction v is r(t) = P + tv, t ∈ R. If every component of v is
nonzero, eliminating t gives (x − P )/v = (y − P )/v = (z − P )/v . If v = 0, retain the

To intersect a line with a plane, substitute its parameterization into the plane equation. Two
spatial lines can be parallel, intersecting, coincident, or skew: skew lines are nonparallel and do
not intersect. When testing intersection use independent parameters for the two lines; equating
their parameters without justification can miss intersections.
For nonparallel directions u, v, the distance between lines P + tu and Q + sv is |(Q − P) ·
(u × v)|/∥u × v∥. The unit common normal measures the invariant perpendicular separation;
components along either line can be removed by choosing t, s. A nonzero numerator detects
skewness, while zero gives intersecting nonparallel lines.

question.text:
For what value of a do the lines (x, y, z) = (t, 1 + t, 2 − t) and (x, y, z) = (1 + s, 2 − s, a + 2s)
intersect?
(A) −1 (B) 0 (C) 1 (D) 2 (E) 3

solution.text:
The first two coordinate equations give t = 1 + s and 1 + t = 2 − s, so s = 0, t = 1. The third
coordinates are then 1 and a, requiring a = 1.

question.text:
Which symmetric description gives the entire line (x, y, z) = (2, 1, −3) + t(0, 3, −2)?
(A) x = 2, (y − 1)/3 = (z + 3)/(−2)
(B) (y − 1)/3 = (z + 3)/(−2) with no restriction on x
(C) x = 2, (y − 1)/2 = (z + 3)/(−3)
(D) x = 2, (y + 1)/3 = (z − 3)/(−2)
(E) x = 0, (y − 1)/3 = (z + 3)/(−2)

solution.text:
The zero first direction component means x stays exactly 2. Eliminating t from the other
coordinates gives the stated ratio equality. Omitting x = 2 would describe a plane, not the
original line; division by the zero component is not allowed.

question.text:
How are the lines r = (1, 2, 3) + t(1, −1, 2) and r = (3, 0, 7) + s(−2, 2, −4) related?
(A) They are skew.
(B) They are distinct and parallel.
(C) They intersect at exactly one point.
(D) They coincide.
(E) They are perpendicular.

solution.text:
The second direction is −2 times the first, and its base point is the first line's point at
t = 2. Indeed the second parametrization equals the first with t = 2 − 2s, which ranges
over every real value. Parallel direction vectors alone would not distinguish coincident from
distinct parallel lines.
